body.heading: Every couple has an origin story
paragraphs: Somewhere in your shared history is a first meeting, a first conversation, a moment one of you decided. Retelling that story — on an anniversary, on a long drive, when a child asks — is not nostalgia for its own sake. It is a reminder, delivered by the two people who know, that the relationship was chosen and could be chosen again.
You will find you remember it differently. That is not a problem to solve; it is half the pleasure. Her version has the rain, his version has the joke, and the true story is the two versions braided.

body.heading: Ask for the details
paragraphs: Prompt each other past the headlines: what were you wearing, what did you think in the first five minutes, when did you tell a friend about it, what nearly went wrong. Small details are where the story lives, and they surface new ones in each other's memory.
Tell it to your children when they are old enough to ask, and to new friends who only know you as a pair. A couple's story, told well, is a small gift to the people who love them.

body.heading: Keep adding chapters
paragraphs: The origin story is chapter one, not the whole book. Retell the later chapters too — the hard year you got through, the ridiculous holiday, the house move. A relationship that narrates itself kindly tends to understand itself kindly.
Write the story down somewhere, in both versions, disagreements included. It is the founding document of your family, and founding documents deserve an archive.

description: Retelling how you met — with all the differing details — reminds a couple that their story was chosen, and is still being written.
